procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated February 9, 1968, in O.P. No. 5032 of 1967 (Contempt), convicting E. M. S. Namboodiripad for contempt of court and sentencing him to Rs. 1000 fine or one month simple imprisonment.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court initiated contempt proceedings against E. M. S. Namboodiripad, calling upon him to show cause why he should not be committed for contempt. He filed an affidavit stating the reports were substantially correct, pleaded lack of intention to disrespect the judiciary, and claimed justification based on freedom of speech. A majority of the High Court (Raman Nair and Krishnamoorthy Iyer JJ.) convicted him, with Mathew J. dissenting. The High Court certified the case as fit for appeal to the Supreme Court under Art. 134(1)(c) of the Constitution.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: E. M. S. Namboodiripad appealed to the Supreme Court against his conviction and sentence. The Supreme Court upheld the appellant's conviction.

directions: The sentence of fine is reduced to Rs. 50/-.
In default of payment of fine, the appellant will undergo simple imprisonment for one week.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant's statements are protected under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, or if they constitute contempt of court.

facts: The appellant made statements at a press conference, which led to contempt of court proceedings.

The appellant argued that his remarks were an exposition of his political ideology, based on the teachings of Marx and Engels, and were therefore protected by his constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression.
law: Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution guarantees the freedom of speech and expression.
The second clause of Article 19 explicitly allows for restrictions on this freedom in relation to contempt of court.
Articles 129 and 215 of the Constitution grant the Supreme Court and High Courts the power to punish for contempt of themselves.
The law of contempt punishes acts or words that tend to obstruct the administration of justice or scandalize the court by bringing it into disrespect or disrepute.
The test for contempt is not the intention of the speaker, but the tendency or likely effect of the words used.
application: The Court acknowledged that while freedom of speech is a fundamental right, it is not absolute and is subject to the restrictions laid out in the Constitution itself, including the law of contempt.
The Court reasoned that the right to freedom of speech cannot be used to abolish the law of contempt or to condone attacks on judges and courts.

The appellant's justification that his statements were based on his political philosophy was deemed irrelevant. The Court stated that the key consideration was the likely effect of his words on the public's perception of the judiciary.
The Court found that the appellant's statements had the clear tendency to lower the prestige and authority of judges and the courts in the eyes of the people.
Therefore, the Court determined that the appellant's speech crossed the line from protected expression into contempt of court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that his statements were not protected under Article 19(1)(a). The Court concluded that the constitutional guarantee of free speech does not protect statements that have the tendency to scandalize the court and lower its authority, regardless of the speaker's intent or ideological justification.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant's statements are protected under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, or if they constitute contempt of court.
appellant_arguments: The statements are protected by the guarantee of freedom of speech and expression under the Constitution.
There was no intention to show disrespect to the judiciary.
The observations made were merely an expression of Marxist philosophy and the program of the Communist Party of India (Marxist), based on the teachings of Marx, Engels, and Lenin.
respondent_arguments: The appellant's statements, which described the judiciary as an 'instrument of oppression' and judges as 'dominated by class hatred, class interests and class prejudices,' directly attack the judiciary.
These statements tend to bring the authority and administration of the law into disrespect and scandalize the court, which constitutes contempt.

statutes.principle: It guarantees the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression.
It allows for the imposition of reasonable restrictions on the freedom of speech and expression in relation to contempt of court.
It specifically confers on the Supreme Court the power to punish for contempt of itself.
It specifically confers on the High Courts the power to punish for contempt of themselves.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The law punishes not only acts which in fact interfere with the courts and administration of justice but also those which have that tendency, that is to say, are likely to produce a particular result.
obiter: For those who think that the laws are defective, the path of reform is open but in a democracy such as ours to weaken the judiciary is to weaken democracy itself.
Where the law is silent the courts have discretion.
The existence of law containing its own guiding principles, reduces the discretion of courts to a minimum.
The courts must do their duty according to their own understanding of the laws and the obligations of the Constitution.
An attempt to shake the people's confidence in the courts is to strike at the very root of our system of democracy.
The courts in India owe their existence, powers and jurisdictions to the Constitution and the laws.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The law of contempt punishes not only acts which do in fact interfere with the courts and administration of justice but also those which have that tendency, that is to say, are likely to produce a particular result. Judged from this angle, there is not a semblance of doubt that the appellant was guilty of contempt of court. Whether he misunderstood the teachings of Marx and Engels or deliberately distorted them is not to much purpose. The likely effect of his words must be seen and they have clearly the effect of lowering the prestige of judges and courts in the eyes of the people.
legal_tests_applied: The test for contempt of court is whether the words or acts either obstruct or tend to obstruct the administration of justice. The law punishes not only acts which do in fact interfere with the courts and administration of justice but also those which have that tendency, that is to say, are likely to produce a particular result.

The right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) is subject to the limitations in Article 19(2), which explicitly allows for reasonable restrictions in relation to contempt of court.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's right to freedom of speech is not absolute; the Constitution itself imposes restrictions in relation to contempt of court, and it cannot be said that the right abolishes the law of contempt.

The appellant's intention is irrelevant to the question of guilt. The court stated, 'That he did not intend any such result may be a matter for consideration in the sentence to he imposed on him but cannot serve as a justification.'

The likely effect of the appellant's words was to lower the prestige of judges and courts in the eyes of the people, which is sufficient to establish contempt, regardless of whether they actually interfered with the administration of justice.
The appellant's position as a Chief Minister and the context of a press conference were considered, as his words would cause mischief due to the belief people would have in them.
why_respondent_won: The appellant's statements constituted scandalising the court, a form of contempt which occurs when a person's conduct tends to bring the authority and administration of the law into disrespect or disregard.
The court found that the appellant's words clearly had the effect of lowering the prestige of judges and courts in the eyes of the people, which satisfies the tendency test for contempt.
policy_considerations: The good faith of the judges is the firm bed-rock on which any system of administration securely rests and an attempt to shake the people's confidence in the courts is to strike at the very root of our system of democracy.
For those who think that the laws are defective, the path of reform is open but in a democracy such as ours to weaken the judiciary is to weaken democracy itself.

The courts must do their duty according to their own understanding of the laws and the obligations of the Constitution. They cannot take their cue from sentiments of politicians nor ever indirectly give support to something which they consider to be wrong against the Constitution and the laws.
